newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: India, Pakistan signal willingness for better ties.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan signal willingness for better ties.

text.p: Pakistan and India have signalled willingness to improve their acrimonious relationship after newly-elected Nawaz Sharif takes power in Islamabad.
But mending a quarrel that casts a nuclear shadow over South Asia will require patient, quiet diplomacy and new flexibility on Kashmir, the key obstacle to neighbourly ties, analysts said.

Sharif, who led the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) to a stunning election triumph on Monday, said his party was committed to "improving relations with India through dialogue and not through confrontation".
"We have to learn how to live as good neighbours. Now is the time for serious dialogue," newspapers quoted him as saying on the eve of the polls.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda responded on Wednesday, saying he favoured resuming high-level talks with Pakistan but would wait for Sharif to take the first step.
Senior members of Sharif's team declined to elaborate on his overture, saying the new government should be formed first.
One PML source said a twin-track approach, involving private as well as public talks, similar to that pursued by Israel and the Palestinians to produce the Oslo accords, might pay off.
"Any successful negotiation requires a lot of behind-the- scenes efforts," he said.
The source, who asked not to be named, said a third country, preferably the United States, could play the same sort of hidden mediating role as Norway had in the Middle East peace talks.
"In a quiet way, not in the glare of publicity. Otherwise, even if you don't make any concessions, somebody will criticise you and you will back-track," he said.
"I think the Indians now realise they have to find a political solution. They can't solve the problem militarily. But how far they are ready to go will depend on the pressures.
"Of course they would very much like to shelve the issue and get on with other things, but how can we accept that?"
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robin Raphel said last month that Washington was ready to help India and Pakistan find a negotiated solution, but only if asked by both sides to do so.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since they were carved out of British India in a bloody partition in 1947. Two of them have been over Kashmir, which is divided between the two nations.

U.S. intelligence officials told the Senate Intelligence Committee on Wednesday that the two countries could stumble into an unwanted war that could rapidly escalate and said they saw few signs that pointed toward a serious thaw.
Pakistan has insisted in the past that mainly Moslem Kashmiris be allowed to vote in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.

India, which says Kashmir is an integral part of its territory, refuses to discuss any change in its status and accuses Pakistan of backing Moslem rebels fighting a seven-year-old separatist revolt in Indian-held Kashmir.
Governments in both countries have stirred nationalist feelings on Kashmir for domestic political reasons, making it that much harder for either to make concessions.
"I am not soft on India, but realistic," Sharif, long seen as a hard-liner on India, was quoted on Thursday as saying.

"Obviously we don't expect the Kashmir issue to be solved in three months," the PML source said. The new government would be looking for "some progress, some acceptance of certain principles, some time-frame, some change in the status quo".
Sharif, backed by the biggest parliamentary majority in Pakistan's recent history, may be better placed than his predecessor, Benazir Bhutto, to take bold steps on India.
Bhutto exchanged letters with Gowda about a possible resumption of talks in mid-1996, but Pakistan backed off when India went ahead with state assembly elections in Kashmir.
The religious Jamaat-i-Islami party, which boycotted Monday's election but was once a PML ally, opposes any talks with New Delhi unless India softens its stand on Kashmir.
"There can be no trade or talks with India unless it accepts that the part of Kashmir it controls is disputed territory," the group's chief Qazi Hussain Ahmad thundered on Wednesday.

In India, nationalists reacted angrily this week to a reported proposal by Farooq Abdullah, chief minister of India's Jammu and Kashmir state, that the ceasefire line dividing Kashmir should be recognised as a permanent border.
Pakistan is committed under the World Trade Organisation to granting India Most Favoured Nation status, but says it needs more time to study the implications of liberalising trade.

"Both countries would benefit," caretaker Commerce Minister Zubair Khan told Reuters last week. "But there are political dimensions which are extremely important in our case. Do the political costs outweigh the economic benefits?"
